_about: Every visitor-facing string of the Standards section: the Standards Cascade, the overview of standards and the page of each standard, checked by the style gate. The questions, ledes, the method note and the overview's strings (5 October 2026) are drafts until Swann has reviewed them. The strings for the choice of standards body (bodyLabel to overviewCascadeLink, 5 October 2026) are drafts for Swann's approval too.

copy.question: Who names NIST’s post-quantum standards, and since when?

copy.method: Each line in the Cascade joins NIST to a government and stands for the institutional documents in which that government names a post-quantum standard in one way; its weight shows how many documents there are, and each document is placed at the date it carries. A document that names several standards counts once on each line it belongs to. The Cascade records references; it is no proof that anything is deployed. A government adopts a standard when its document says it uses or requires it; it adds national requirements when it adopts the standard with conditions of its own, such as mandatory hybrid schemes or national certification; it names a standard when it refers to it without adopting it; it runs its own process when it builds national algorithms. Lines run from NIST only for the standards NIST has published or selected; a document naming another body’s standard is listed in the table. Colour shows the bloc a government coordinates with, as on the Atlas map, and on the orbit the marker shape shows its standards role. The lines rest on {lineDocs} of the {corpusSize} institutional documents the Atlas holds. A missing line means the Atlas has not recorded such a document; it does not mean none exists.

copy.questionBody: Who names {body} post-quantum standards, and since when?
copy.ledeBody: Each government is placed at the date of its first institutional document naming one of them. Every body’s standards, with the governments that cite them, are in the Overview.
copy.bodyNote: The {body} citations come from a targeted reading of 27 documents, not a systematic pass like NIST’s, so a government not marked here may still cite these standards, and this view is never a ranking.

copy.methodBody: Each line in this view joins the centre to a government and stands for the institutional documents in which that government names {body} post-quantum standards in one way; its weight shows how many documents there are, and each document is placed at the date it carries. A document that names several standards counts once on each line it belongs to. The view records references; it is no proof that anything is deployed. The globe and the map draw no lines, because where a standards body is based says nothing about who cites it, and a standards body’s own document never counts as a government citing it. The national processes belong to the NIST view. The lines rest on {lineDocs} of the {corpusSize} institutional documents the Atlas holds, found in a targeted reading of 27 documents rather than a systematic pass like NIST’s. A missing line means the Atlas has not recorded such a document; it does not mean none exists.
